s: The rotten vegetables' lair, a comical compost-heap underworld of earthy strata, buried junk and mouldy glowing toadstools.
A deep indigo cavern lit almost only by living things, with candy-coloured cyan, magenta and lime toadstools glowing out of the dark.
The entrance hall of an ancient vegetable kingdom's vault, mossy stone and roots in green darkness, lit by a sealed gold-glowing door.
The final boss chamber deep in the roots of a colossal carrot, giant amber taproots rising to a glowing heart above plum-dark soil.
A cosy rabbit warren of warm brown soil just under the garden, with carrot taproots poking through and amber glow-caps for light.
A dead bhut jolokia come back as a cartoon ghost. It floats, phases through bullets, teleports behind you, breathes ghost fire and looses homing wisps. The burrow's bottom-room boss.
The Ginger's immune spectral projection. It haunts whichever boss room the squad is fighting in and harasses the players there with telegraphed bolt fans.
A flying ginger-root sorcerer that rules the burrow's hub. It can't be hurt until the squad brings back the three key orbs, and every orb unlocks more of its health and more of its fury.

The middle-room boss of the Burrow Encounter, a towering red-and-black ear of corn that sprays scissoring kernel streams, lobs popcorn mortars that leave burning patches, and slams its husk into the ground.
The top-room boss of the Burrow Encounter, a huge rosy sweet potato bull that chains charges into the walls, sends shockwaves along the floor and ambushes from underground.
How the carrot is drawn and brought to life: a per-pixel shaded body with a face, a cape, gold epaulettes, a belt and floating boots that all move as it runs, jumps and dashes.
A quick horizontal burst that makes the carrot untouchable for its whole length, so you can dash straight through attacks.
Every carrot has a recharging shield over its health. Hits drain the shield first; once it breaks, hits cost health, and at 0 health the carrot is knocked down.
How the carrot runs, sprints, jumps, double jumps and drops through planks, on fixed-step platformer physics.
The first dungeon encounter, in the Warm Burrow. Clear three sealed boss rooms, carry each boss's orb back to the hub, then bring down The Ginger to open the way deeper.
A tall asparagus sniper that drops onto a high perch, puffs up its cheeks behind a laser sight and spits a glowing scale at you.
The Corn Ogre, a giant ear of corn in a husk jacket that stumbles after players, peels its husk open and sprays a sweeping volley of red-hot kernels.
A portobello outlaw with a pistol in each hand that keeps its distance, takes aim and fires short bursts of slow glowing slugs.
A big hot-headed chili brute that lobs fireballs from afar, advances step by step, and breathes fire at point-blank range.
A lumpy potato on four stubby legs that paws the ground, charges in a straight line, and is left stunned and open if it slams into a wall.
A jack-o'-lantern on stubby vine legs that sprints at the nearest player, lights its fuse and blows itself up.
A rotten carrot that shambles toward the nearest player with its arms out and slaps them.
The original one-screen fighting ground on a sunny hillside, with three wooden planks over the grass.
A big scrolling test cave in the Warm Burrow look, built to try out the following camera, fixed camera shots and the biome parts.
Work in progress: the game opens in a sunny vegetable garden, where the carrots walk past a giant carrot and jump down a mushroom-lined hole into the burrow.
The building blocks every level is made of, placed and tuned in the Godot 2D editor. Ground, ledges, mushrooms, doors, pedestals, torches, camera shots, spawn markers and props.

The opening of the game, timed to its music. A star screen doubles as the lobby, a shooting star starts the song, the carrots walk to a cliff above a sea of clouds, the logo booms in, and everyone leaps.
Destiny-style ammo: normal never runs out, special and heavy come from bricks dropped by dead enemies.
The camera follows your own carrot, Terraria-style, leads ahead when you fall, and switches to a fixed shot inside arenas and boss rooms.
One to three players fight together online, and the game also runs in a browser. Each player runs their own carrot; the host runs the enemies.
How much hits hurt, on both sides. Every carrot has a shield over its health, guns get weaker with range, and dashes dodge everything.
Regular enemies wear their name over their head with a little health bar. Bosses get a big name-and-health bar at the bottom of the screen instead, which shows when they're shielded or partly locked.
Outside raid encounters, a level keeps a set roster of enemies about. Each arrives in turn from the edges, and each one killed is replaced by another of its kind.

How a boss room's fight is paced in beats. Each beat brings a hand-picked squad of enemies in at one of the room's spawn groups when its trigger fires, so a fight rises and falls the way it was drawn.
Esc or P freezes the game for everyone in the squad. Press either again to carry on.
How the guns reload, what each reload looks and sounds like, the reload bar under the crosshair, and what your co-op partners see.
The carrot's grenade, a crackling plasma orb that's lobbed, bounces, and bursts in an electric shockwave.
A six-shooter sidearm, precise and hard-hitting, with almost no damage falloff.
One rocket, one huge explosion, then the slowest reload in the game.
A pump-action that fans out a blast of pellets, strongest point-blank and weak at range.
A full-auto hose with a big magazine, deadly up close and nearly harmless at range.
The bottom-left readout of your energy ball's recharge, the rounds in your gun and its name.

Gameplay numbers for the Ghost Pepper boss (scripts/ghost_pepper.gd): health, the float, the five powers (phase, teleport, ghost-fire breath, homing wisps, the enrage and its clones) and the juice. Every ghost pepper shares one of these (styles/enemies/ghost_pepper.tres); edit it in the Inspector, or live via the Remote tree. Players have 100 health; enemy HP is in revolver units (a body shot does 10, a headshot 20).

Numbers for the Ginger Shade (scripts/ginger_shade.gd): The Ginger's immune spectral projection that haunts whichever boss room is fighting. Every shade shares one of these (styles/enemies/ginger_shade.tres); edit it in the Inspector, or live via the Remote tree. Players have 100 health.

Gameplay numbers for The Ginger, the burrow encounter's main boss (scripts/ginger.gd): its health and how the pedestal orbs unlock it, the float, the taunting immune phase, the transformation, the four attacks (purple bombs, magic bolts, floor eruptions, the root sweep), the shield, the enrage and the juice. Every ginger shares one of these (styles/enemies/ginger.tres); edit it in the Inspector, or live via the Remote tree. Players have 100 health; enemy HP is in revolver units (a body shot does 10, a headshot 20).

Gameplay numbers for the Big Red-and-Black Corn boss (scripts/red_corn.gd): health, its heavy stumbling gait, the husk telegraph, the twin kernel streams and fans, the popcorn mortars and their burning patches, the husk slam and the enrage. One shared resource (styles/enemies/red_corn.tres); edit it in the Inspector, or live via the Remote tree. Players have 100 health; enemy HP is in revolver units (a body shot does 10, a headshot 20).

Movement feel for anything that runs on platformer physics: the player carrots (tuning.tres) and each walking enemy (<kind>_tuning.tres). Some fields only matter for players and say so. While the game runs from the editor, select a carrot in the Remote scene tree to edit these live.

Gameplay and feel numbers for the Sweet Potato boss (scripts/sweet_potato.gd). The default instance is styles/enemies/sweet_potato.tres; tweak it in the Inspector (or live on the boss in the Remote tree). Enemy HP is in revolver units: a body shot does 10, a headshot 20. A carrot runs at 115 px/s.

Feel knobs for the carrots' hero gear and face: the floating boots' walk cycle and footsteps, how the cape, epaulette tassels and belt strap swing, and where the face and gear sit on the body. Shared by every player via styles/gear_tuning.tres. Heights are in pixels up from the carrot's tip (the body is 36 tall; the leaves start at about 34).
A carrot's colours. Each player slot gets one (see styles/). Edit the .tres files to recolour.

How a carrot's shield breaking, staying down and recharging looks and sounds (the numbers it runs on are in styles/tuning.tres: Shield and health). Lives in styles/shield_look.tres.

How your own shield and health show: the bars at the top of the screen and the red "jelly" that creeps in from the screen's edges as your health runs low. Lives in styles/player_hud.tres. (The numbers they show are in styles/tuning.tres: Shield and health.)
The colours of an encounter's keys: each boss room's torches, the buff its boss drops and the hub pedestal it belongs on all share one colour, so players can tell which goes where.
Gameplay numbers for the asparagus (the perched sniper that spits its scales). Every asparagus shares styles/enemies/asparagus.tres; edit it in the Inspector, or live via the Remote tree.

Every corn shares one of these (styles/enemies/corn.tres); edit it in the Inspector, or live via the Remote tree. Players have 100 health; enemy HP is in revolver units (a body shot does 10).

Timing knobs for the title sequence (scripts/title.gd), shared by every machine via styles/title_timing.tres. Edit it in the Inspector and save, then press R in a running debug game: the title reloads with the new numbers (the host's R replays it for everyone). Or, while running from the editor, select Title in the Remote scene tree and edit its timing live.

Destiny-style ammo bricks: every enemy that dies may drop a special (green) or heavy (purple) brick, at most one per kill. The host rolls each drop and tells every machine; each player gets their own copy that only they can pick up, so partners never fight over ammo. Lives in styles/ammo_drops.tres; every number is a slider.
What every enemy is called, which kinds are bosses, and how their names and health show.

How much each enemy kind adds to a fight: its threat cost. A Squad's threat is the sum over its members, and each BossRoom shows its beats' threat so the fight's difficulty curve can be read without playing. One shared table (styles/threat_costs.tres); bosses aren't counted.

The energy ball every carrot carries (G or right mouse): a crackling plasma orb that's lobbed, bounces, and bursts in an electric shockwave. How it's thrown, how it flies, how big the burst is, how fast it recharges and its colours. Lives in styles/grenade.tres; every number is a slider.

One gun: how it handles, how its damage falls off with range, and how it looks and sounds. Each lives in styles/weapons/ as a .tres you can tune in the Inspector (every number is a slider; "or_greater" sliders accept typed values past their end). While the game runs from the editor, edit the .tres live and the next shot uses the new numbers. Weapon.all() lists them in the order the number keys pick them.

How the bottom-left weapon HUD looks: the grenade recharge icon, the ammo pips and the gun's name. Lives in styles/hud.tres.

The guns every carrot carries into a level, in the order the number keys pick them (1, 2, 3...) and Q cycles them. Lives in styles/loadout.tres; drag a Weapon from styles/weapons/ in or out to change it. (Weapon.all() is still every gun the game knows, in network order; the loadout only picks which of them you hold.)
